feature: ingest_change orchestration (diff -> scan -> store -> chain)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want a single entry point that takes a code diff plus its attribution and runs the full governance pipeline so that every AI- or human-authored change is scanned, recorded, and entered into the audit trail in one atomic, auditable step.
expected_behavior: ingest_change(store, chain, org, repo, diff, attribution, sha=None) -> dict orchestrates the whole pipeline. It (0) validates the tenant up front via _tenant_key(org) (ingest.py:96) - a blank/whitespace/zero-width or |-containing org raises ValueError before any diff parsing or store/chain write; (1) calls parse_diff(diff) to get per-file added lines; (2) runs scan_lines(path, added) for each file, accumulating a list[Finding]; (3) builds a human summary string f'{len(files)} file(s) changed; {len(findings)} finding(s)'; (4) persists the change via store.add_change(org, repo, sha, attribution.author, attribution.agent, summary) to get change_id; (5) writes each finding via store.add_finding(change_id, org, repo, f.as_row()); (6) backfills the finding count via store.set_change_findings(org, change_id, len(findings)) - an org-scoped UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND org=?, so a cross-tenant update matches 0 rows; (7) appends a tamper-evident entry to chain.append(org, payload) where payload carries change_id, repo, sha, author, agent, the list of changed file paths, and a redacted findings list whose entries have keys exactly {check, severity, file, line} (the payload key is 'check', not 'check_id') - no raw snippet or secret fragment reaches the ledger (proven by test_chain_payload_carries_redacted_findings_no_snippet). Returns {change_id, findings, n_findings, chain_seq, files} where chain_seq is the per-org sequence number from the chain entry.
edge_cases: Empty/no-op diff: parse_diff returns [], no scan runs, findings=[], n_findings=0, but a change row and a chain entry are STILL created (summary '0 file(s) changed; 0 finding(s)') - so even a clean change is recorded in the audit trail. || Clean change with files but zero findings: set_change_findings(change_id, 0) is still called and a chain entry with an empty findings list is appended, proving the change was scanned and passed. || sha=None (uncommitted/pre-commit ingest): the change and chain payload record sha as null; ingest still succeeds because sha is optional and only used as a reference field. || Invalid org (empty, invisible-only, or containing |): ValueError from _tenant_key before any store or chain write.
notes: Orchestration is intentionally thin: it delegates parsing, scanning, persistence, and chaining to dedicated modules (parse_diff, safety.engine.scan_lines, GovernanceStore, GovernanceChain). The chain entry deliberately omits snippets because redaction happens upstream in the engine.

feature: parse_diff - extract added lines with real new-file line numbers
user_story: As a developer, I want only the lines my change actually adds to be scanned, each tagged with its true line number in the new file, so that safety findings point me at the exact line I introduced rather than at diff offsets or unrelated context.
expected_behavior: parse_diff(diff: str) -> list[tuple[str, list[tuple[int, str]]]] walks a unified diff line by line and returns one tuple per file: (file_path, [(new_line_number, added_text), ...]). It tracks the current file from '+++ ' headers, stripping a leading 'b/' prefix; resets new_lineno from each '@@' hunk header by regex-matching the new-side start (r'\+(\d+)'); records each '+' added line (excluding the '+++' header) as (new_lineno, raw[1:]) and increments new_lineno; advances new_lineno on context lines (those starting with a single space); and does NOT advance the new-side counter on '-' removed lines. Only added lines are captured (that is what the change introduces); removed and context lines are not scanned.
edge_cases: New-file deletions ('+++ /dev/null'): cur_file is set to None for that target, so a fully deleted file contributes no scannable added lines. || Multiple hunks in one file: each '@@' header re-seeds new_lineno from its own new-side start, so line numbers stay correct across non-contiguous hunks within the same file. || Malformed/absent '@@' new-side number: the regex falls back to new_lineno=0 (m is None -> 0), so added lines in a header-less or malformed hunk are still captured but numbered from 0 rather than crashing.
notes: The single-space context branch ('elif raw.startswith(" ")') is what keeps line numbers honest across context regions; removed lines are explicitly a no-op on the counter (lines 67-68).

feature: infer_attribution - detect authoring agent from commit trailers
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want the system to automatically identify which AI agent (or a human) authored a change from its commit-message trailers so that the audit trail attributes every change without relying on engineers to self-report.
expected_behavior: infer_attribution(commit_message: str, author: str = 'unknown') -> Attribution scans the commit message against the _AGENT_TRAILERS table of case-insensitive regexes and returns Attribution(author=author, agent=<matched agent>). Recognized trailers: 'Co-Authored-By: Claude' -> agent='claude'; 'Co-Authored-By: ChatGPT|GPT|OpenAI' -> 'gpt'; 'Co-Authored-By: [GitHub ]Copilot' -> 'copilot'; 'Co-Authored-By: Cursor' -> 'cursor'. If no trailer matches, it defaults to Attribution(author, agent='human'). Attribution is a dataclass with author (default 'unknown') and agent (default 'unknown') fields; this attribution feeds directly into ingest_change via attribution.author and attribution.agent.
edge_cases: None or empty commit_message: guarded by `commit_message or ''`, so a None message does not raise and yields agent='human'. || Dict iteration order determines precedence: a message containing BOTH a Claude and a GPT trailer returns the first match in _AGENT_TRAILERS order ('claude' before 'gpt'), not a multi-agent result. || Unknown agent (e.g. 'Co-Authored-By: Gemini'): no pattern matches, so it is classified as 'human' - a new agent vendor silently collapses into the human bucket until its trailer pattern is added.
notes: Attribution can also be supplied directly by the caller (an org's CI knows who ran), per the module docstring; infer_attribution is the fallback path when only a commit message is available.

feature: Agent-agnostic treatment (claude/gpt/cursor/copilot/human identical)
source: governance/ingest.py module docstring (lines 1-8) + ingest_change (lines 78-117); attribution is recorded metadata, never a control branch
user_story: As an auditor/regulator, I want every change scanned by the same grounded safety checks regardless of whether Claude, GPT, Cursor, Copilot, or a human produced it, so that no authoring source gets a weaker (or harsher) review and the governance bar is provably uniform.
expected_behavior: Agent-agnosticism is structural, not a feature flag: ingest_change operates on the diff *output* and an attribution string, and there is NO branch anywhere in the pipeline that varies parsing, scanning, storage, or chaining by attribution.agent. parse_diff -> scan_lines -> store.add_change/add_finding -> chain.append run identically for every value of agent. The agent value is carried purely as recorded metadata: store.add_change(..., attribution.agent, ...) writes it to the changes row and chain.append embeds 'agent' in the tamper-evident payload. The same code path applies whether agent is 'claude', 'gpt', 'copilot', 'cursor', 'human', or any other/unknown string.
edge_cases: agent='unknown' (Attribution defaults) or any unrecognized vendor string: treated exactly like a recognized agent - full scan, full store, full chain entry; the unknown label is simply recorded, never used to skip or escalate checks. || Human-authored change (agent='human'): receives the identical scan and audit treatment as any AI agent - the layer governs humans and agents on the same path. || Same diff ingested twice under different agents: produces identical findings (scan depends only on file path + added lines), differing solely in the recorded agent/author metadata and the new change_id/chain_seq.
notes: This is the 'agnostic backbone' claim from the docstring: by parsing the diff rather than hooking a specific tool, the layer works for any AI agent or human producer without per-vendor integration.

feature: Multi-tenant org + repo isolation
source: governance/ingest.py:ingest_change (org/repo threaded into store.add_change line 94, store.add_finding line 96, chain.append line 101); chain.py:append (lines 31-38) using store.chain_head(org)
user_story: As a platform operator, I want each organization's changes, findings, and audit chain kept isolated by org (and tagged by repo) so that one tenant can never read, pollute, or break another tenant's governance records on shared infrastructure.
expected_behavior: Every persistence and audit call in ingest_change is scoped by org and tagged by repo. store.add_change(org, repo, sha, ...) writes the org and repo onto the changes row; store.add_finding(change_id, org, repo, finding) carries org+repo onto each finding row; and chain.append(org, payload) appends to a PER-ORG hash chain - chain.append derives its head via store.chain_head(org), increments that org's own seq, and links to that org's own prev_hash (GENESIS for a new org). The returned chain_seq is therefore the sequence number within the org's chain, independent of other orgs. repo is recorded inside the change row, finding rows, and the chain payload, giving per-repo tagging within a tenant.
edge_cases: First change for a brand-new org: store.chain_head(org) yields seq 0 / no prev, so chain.append links to GENESIS and returns chain_seq=1 - each org's chain starts fresh and independently. || Concurrent ingests across two different orgs: each appends to its own org-scoped chain head, so their sequence numbers and prev_hash links never interleave or collide. || Same repo name under two different orgs (e.g. both have 'api'): isolation is by org, so identical repo strings in different tenants remain separate records and separate chains - repo alone is not a tenant boundary.
notes: Isolation hinges on org being the chain partition key (chain_head(org)/append_chain(org,...)); repo is a secondary tag, not an isolation boundary. ingest_change itself does not enforce that the caller-supplied org is authorized - that authorization is expected upstream (e.g. webhook/CLI token), consistent with this layer being the thin orchestrator.

feature: Two-signal detect->verify gate (scan_lines)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want every flagged line to clear two independent signals before it becomes a finding so that my team triages real risks instead of drowning in regex false positives from any AI agent's diff.
expected_behavior: scan_lines(file: str, added_lines: list[tuple[int, str]]) -> list[Finding] iterates each (lineno, text) pair against every Check in CHECKS. For each check it runs signal 1, chk.detect.search(text); if no match it continues (detect absent). On a match it runs signal 2, chk.verify(text, m); if verify returns False the candidate is dropped (verify refutes). Only when BOTH detect fires AND verify confirms does it construct a Finding and append it. verify is an independent second signal that does not share detect's failure mode (e.g. _verify_secret refutes env-var reads and placeholders, _verify_sql refutes parameterized/constant queries, _verify_xss refutes constant-literal assignments). A line can yield multiple findings (one per passing check). Each Finding sets verified=True.
edge_cases: A line matches a check's detect but verify refutes it (e.g. password = os.environ['PW'] hits the secret detector but _verify_secret sees the _ENV_REF and returns False) -> no finding emitted. || A single added line trips several checks (e.g. an http:// URL built from an interpolated user variable) -> scan_lines appends one Finding per check whose detect+verify both pass. || An empty added_lines list or lines where no detect fires -> returns an empty list (no findings), not an error.

feature: Grounding cite() enforcement (no source, no finding)
user_story: As an auditor/regulator, I want every safety finding to carry a citation to an authoritative framework (OWASP/CWE/GDPR) so that I can trace each flagged risk to a named, versioned standard rather than an opaque tool opinion.
expected_behavior: Before a Finding is built, scan_lines calls cite(chk.framework). cite(framework_id: str) -> dict looks up framework_id in the GROUNDING registry; if absent it raises KeyError('ungrounded check references unknown framework ...'), so an ungrounded check cannot produce a finding (no source, no finding). On a hit it returns {'framework': g['name'], 'framework_url': g['url'], 'clause': framework_id}. scan_lines copies these into the Finding's framework, framework_url, and clause fields, so every emitted finding carries the authoritative source name, canonical URL, and the framework id as the clause. GROUNDING entries also carry version and last_verified stamps (a later release gate re-fetches the URLs to defeat citation theater).
edge_cases: A check is added with a framework id not registered in GROUNDING -> cite() raises KeyError at scan time and the scan fails loudly rather than silently emitting an uncited finding. || Two distinct checks share one framework id (e.g. secret-hardcoded and private-key-hardcoded both cite 'cwe-798') -> cite() returns the same source dict for both; findings differ by check_id but share framework/framework_url/clause. || A GROUNDING url goes stale between releases -> the last_verified stamp / re-fetch gate is the intended detector; cite() itself still returns the (now-stale) registered url.

feature: Secret redaction before storage
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want any secret captured in a flagged code snippet to be redacted before it is stored or reported so that the audit trail itself never becomes a place credentials leak.
expected_behavior: redact(text: str) -> str runs a multi-stage pipeline (engine.py:20-74). Stage 1, _REDACT_TOKEN: known vendor token shapes - AWS AKIA keys, OpenAI sk- keys, Slack xox[baprs]- tokens, GitHub gh[pousr]_/github_pat_ tokens, GitLab glpat- tokens, Google AIza keys, and JWTs (eyJ...eyJ...) - are substituted with the literal '<REDACTED-SECRET>'. Stage 2, _REDACT_ASSIGN: key=value / key: value assignments where the key CONTAINS a secret-ish substring (api_key/secret/token/password/passwd/access_key/client_secret/cred/auth/...) have the quoted value replaced with '<REDACTED>' - substring matching, so non-allowlisted names like my_custom_cred and gitlab_token ARE masked. Stage 3, _REDACT_EMBEDDED: embedded credential forms - URL basic-auth (user:pw@host), secret-bearing query params, bearer tokens, and DB password flags - are masked in place. Stage 4, _REDACT_ENTROPY: a bounded entropy fallback masks quoted high-entropy mixed-class literals of 20+ chars that no earlier pass caught. scan_lines applies redact(text.strip())[:300] to the snippet stored on every Finding, so redaction runs before truncation. The principle: a security scanner that prints the secret it caught is the bug.
edge_cases: A snippet contains a recognized token shape AND an assignment (e.g. api_key = 'ghp_realtoken...') -> both the vendor pass and the assignment pass fire. || A secret assigned to a non-allowlisted key name (e.g. my_custom_cred = '...') IS masked via the secret-ish substring match, and a bare unprefixed 20+ char secret is caught by the entropy fallback (test_entropy_redaction_masks_unprefixed_secret); genuinely unrecognized short or low-entropy formats may still slip past the entropy gate - best-effort, documented in SECURITY-HARDENING.md. || A very long line with the secret beyond character 300 -> after redaction the snippet is truncated to 300 chars; redaction runs before truncation so an early secret is still masked (multiple secret classes on one line all masked: test_redaction_masks_multiple_secret_classes_on_one_line).

feature: Severity classification
source: governance/safety/engine.py:Finding.severity (line 37) populated in scan_lines line 68 from chk.severity (checks.py:Check.severity, line 173)
user_story: As a developer, I want each finding tagged with a severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) so that I can fix blocking issues first and not be forced to treat every flag as equally urgent.
expected_behavior: Severity is a per-check constant declared on the Check (Check.severity: str, one of CRITICAL | HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW). scan_lines copies chk.severity verbatim into Finding.severity at construction (line 68). Examples from the registry: secret-hardcoded and private-key-hardcoded are CRITICAL; sql-injection, xss-unescaped, path-traversal, ssrf, insecure-deserialization are HIGH; pii-in-code, weak-crypto, cleartext-transmission, floating-action-tag are MEDIUM. Severity is deterministic per check id, not computed from the matched text. Finding.as_row() -> dict includes the 'severity' key so the value flows into the stored row / report / dashboard.
edge_cases: The same code line trips two checks of different severity (e.g. a CRITICAL hardcoded-secret and a MEDIUM cleartext-http on one line) -> two findings emit, each carrying its own check's severity; there is no merge into a single max-severity record. || Severity is fixed at the check level, so an objectively low-risk instance of a HIGH-severity check (e.g. SQL interpolation in a test fixture) still reports HIGH; nuance is handled by verify gating presence, not by downgrading severity. || A new check added without a severity value -> Check is a dataclass with severity as a required field, so construction fails fast rather than emitting an unlabeled finding.

feature: Per-finding fix hints
source: governance/safety/engine.py:Finding.fix_hint (line 44) populated in scan_lines line 71 from chk.fix_hint (checks.py:Check.fix_hint, line 177)
user_story: As a developer, I want each finding to come with a concrete remediation hint so that I can resolve the flagged issue without leaving the report to go research the fix.
expected_behavior: fix_hint is a per-check remediation string declared on the Check (Check.fix_hint: str). scan_lines passes chk.fix_hint into the Finding's fix_hint field (line 71). Each hint is specific and actionable to the check, e.g. secret-hardcoded: 'Move the secret to an environment variable / secret manager; rotate it if it was committed.'; sql-injection: 'Use parameterized queries (?, %s, :name) - never interpolate user input into SQL.'; path-traversal: 'Confine to a base dir (resolve + check prefix); use secure_filename / os.path.basename.'; private-key-hardcoded: 'Remove the key from source and ROTATE it immediately; load from a secret manager.' The hint is the same for every instance of a given check (keyed by check id), independent of the matched line.
edge_cases: Finding.fix_hint defaults to '' on the dataclass; every registry Check supplies a non-empty fix_hint, so in practice findings always carry guidance, but a future check omitting it would surface a blank hint rather than an error. || fix_hint is NOT included in Finding.as_row() (as_row exposes check_id/category/severity/file/line/snippet/framework/framework_url/clause/verified) -> consumers that need the hint must read it off the Finding object directly, not from the stored row dict. || The hint is generic-to-the-check, so for a hardcoded-secret finding it always says to rotate 'if committed' even when the redacted snippet can't confirm whether a real (vs placeholder) secret was committed; the verify gate, not the hint, decides whether the finding fires.

feature: secret-hardcoded check (Hard-coded credential)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want any AI- or human-authored diff that hard-codes an API key, token, or password literal to be flagged so that committed credentials are caught before they reach the repo and have to be rotated.
expected_behavior: scan_lines returns a Finding with check_id='secret-hardcoded', category='security', severity='CRITICAL', framework='cwe-798' only when BOTH signals fire. Signal 1 (detect): a regex matching `(api_key|secret|token|password|passwd|access_key|client_secret|credential|auth_token|private_key) [:=] '<val 6+ chars>'` OR a vendor-shaped literal (AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}, sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}, xox[baprs]-..., gh[pousr]_..., github_pat_..., glpat-..., AIza..., JWT eyJ...eyJ...). Signal 2 (independent verify, _verify_secret): refutes the candidate if the line reads from env (_ENV_REF: os.environ/process.env/getenv/${/import.meta.env/config.get), if the captured value matches _PLACEHOLDER (example/xxx/placeholder/your_/change_me/dummy/fake/<...>/secret_key_here/todo/replace_me/redacted/sample/...), or if the alphanumeric substance of the value is < 8 chars. True-positive from tests: `token = "sk-A1B2C3D4E5F6G7H8I9J0K1L2M3N4O5"` fires (test_secret_tp_real_key_fires). Verify-drop: `password = "your_password_here"` is dropped because _PLACEHOLDER matches 'your_' (test_secret_fp_placeholder_dropped_by_verify). True-negative: `api_key = os.environ['API_KEY']` never becomes a finding because _ENV_REF refutes it (test_secret_tn_no_literal).
edge_cases: A real-looking value that happens to contain a placeholder token (e.g. an actual key with 'sample' in it) is suppressed by _PLACEHOLDER even though it is genuine. || A short but real secret (alphanumeric substance < 8 chars) is dropped by the len>=8 substance gate. || A secret assigned from config.get(...) is treated as env-sourced and refuted even if the config itself embeds the literal elsewhere.
notes: Two-signal gate: detect is the candidate, _verify_secret is the independent second signal; neither alone produces a finding. fix_hint: move secret to env/secret manager and rotate if committed. Vendor-format coverage (gh[pousr]_/github_pat_/glpat-/AIza/JWT) and the redacted/sample placeholders proven by test_secret_detect_covers_vendor_formats / test_secret_detect_drops_placeholder_vendor_token (SEC-8).

feature: sql-injection check (SQL built from string interpolation)
user_story: As a developer, I want diffs that build SQL by interpolating variables into a query string to be flagged, while parameterized queries pass, so that I catch injection risk without being nagged about safe DB calls.
expected_behavior: Produces check_id='sql-injection', severity='HIGH', framework='owasp-a03-2021' only when both signals agree. Signal 1 (detect): a call to execute/cursor.execute/.query/db.query/.raw/executemany/executescript wrapping an (optionally f-string) literal containing a SQL keyword (select|insert|update|delete|drop). Signal 2 (_verify_sql, checks.py:69-85): inspects ONLY the first call argument (extracted by _first_call_arg, checks.py:42-66, so a bind-parameter tuple is excluded), masks string literals, and confirms on f-string interpolation (any prefix casing f/F/rf/fR; uppercase variable names match via {[A-Za-z_]...}), .format/.format_map calls, %-formatting applied to the masked expression (any spacing, dict or tuple), or string+variable concatenation on either side. Parameterized queries pass because the placeholder lives inside the masked literal and the bind tuple sits outside the inspected first argument - there is no _PARAM short-circuit. True-positive: cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = {uid}") fires (test_sql_tp_interpolated_query_fires). Verify-drop: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?", (uid,)) is dropped because the bind tuple is excluded from the inspected argument (test_sql_parameterized_like_tuple_not_flagged).
edge_cases: A variable interpolated into the SQL string fires even when a ? bind placeholder also appears on the line - the bind tuple no longer masks the interpolation. || Uppercase interpolated names (e.g. {UID}) ARE matched (test_sql_fstring_uppercase_name_fires); executescript with concatenation fires (test_sql_executescript_concat_fires); %-formatting with no space fires (test_sql_percent_no_space_fires). || Multi-line query construction (concatenation split across lines) still escapes detection because scan is per-line.
notes: Independent second signal is the first-argument literal-masking + interpolation analysis, which does not share detect's failure mode (a constant or parameterized query is dropped). executescript added to the detect sink list per SEC-2.

feature: xss-unescaped check (Unescaped HTML sink)
user_story: As a developer, I want unescaped HTML sinks that receive a variable or expression to be flagged, while sinks fed a constant string literal pass, so that real DOM-injection risk surfaces without false alarms on static markup.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='xss-unescaped', severity='HIGH', framework='cwe-79' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (_XSS_SINK, assembled from string fragments so the file's own source carries no contiguous sink literal): matches dangerouslySetInnerHTML, `.innerHTML =`, or `v-html=`. Signal 2 (_verify_xss): refutes a pure constant assignment  -  if the text after the match is `= '...';` (a quoted literal to end of line) or a `__html: '...'}` constant, it returns False; otherwise a variable/expression is assumed to flow in and it confirms. True-positive: `return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: userInput}} />` fires because the value is the variable userInput, not a constant literal (test_xss_tp_variable_sink_fires). Verify-drop: `el.innerHTML = "static text"` is dropped because the constant-literal-assignment regex matches (test_xss_fp_constant_dropped_by_verify).
edge_cases: A sink assigned a template literal with embedded expression that still looks like a quoted constant could be mis-refuted depending on quote shape. || Concatenated constant + variable (`innerHTML = 'a' + b`) is confirmed because it does not match the pure-constant end-of-line pattern. || Server-side template sinks not matching React/Vue/innerHTML idioms are not covered by _XSS_SINK.
notes: The sink literal is deliberately de-fragmented in source to avoid tripping naive content scanners against checks.py itself  -  the same false-positive class verify() drops.

feature: weak-crypto check (Weak crypto on a credential)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want use of broken hash/cipher primitives (MD5, SHA1, DES, RC4) on credential material to be flagged, while the same primitives used for non-security checksums pass, so that password/token hashing weaknesses are caught without flagging benign cache keys.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='weak-crypto', severity='MEDIUM', framework='cwe-327' only when both signals fire. Signal 1 (detect): word-boundary match on md5|sha1|hashlib.md5|hashlib.sha1|DES|RC4. Signal 2 (_verify_weak_crypto): confirms only if the line also matches _SEC_CTX (password|passwd|pwd|pw|secret|token|credential|auth|api_key/api-key|signature|hmac; pwd and pw are word-bounded, checks.py:29)  -  i.e. the weak primitive is applied in a security context, not a plain checksum. True-positive: `digest = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()` fires because 'password' satisfies _SEC_CTX (test_weak_crypto_tp_on_credential_fires). Verify-drop: `cache_key = hashlib.md5(file_bytes).hexdigest()` is dropped  -  md5 detected but no security-context token on the line (test_weak_crypto_fp_checksum_dropped_by_verify).
edge_cases: A weak hash over credential material whose security-context word lives on a different line is refuted (per-line context only). || A variable named e.g. `auth_cache` triggers _SEC_CTX ('auth') and would confirm even for a non-security checksum. || DES matched as a standalone word could collide with unrelated identifiers, but the _SEC_CTX gate suppresses non-security uses.
notes: The credential-context test is the independent second signal: it does not share detect's failure mode (a checksum over file bytes is dropped).

feature: path-traversal check (File path built from user input)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want file-open/send calls whose path is assembled from user-influenced input to be flagged, while sanitized/confined paths pass, so that directory-traversal exposure in AI-generated file handlers is caught.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='path-traversal', severity='HIGH', framework='cwe-22' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (_PATH_TRAVERSAL): open/send_file/sendfile called with a built path (contains +, f-string, .format, % or os.path.join inside the args). Signal 2 (_verify_path_traversal): first refutes if the line shows sanitization (secure_filename|os.path.basename|.resolve()|realpath|safe_join); otherwise confirms only if a user-influenced token is present (request|param|user|input|filename|file_path|upload|path|payload|args). True-positive: `data = open(upload_dir + filename).read()` fires  -  built path, 'upload'/'filename' present, no sanitizer (test_path_traversal_tp_user_path_fires). Verify-drop: `data = open(os.path.basename(upload_dir + filename)).read()` is dropped because os.path.basename confines it (test_path_traversal_fp_sanitized_dropped).
edge_cases: A path confined by a custom helper not in the sanitizer list is still flagged (no allowlist for bespoke confinement). || A constant built path with no user-influence token (e.g. `open('a/' + 'b')`) is refuted by the user-token requirement. || secure_filename applied on a prior line, with the unsafe open on the next, escapes refutation (per-line).
notes: Independent second signal = sanitizer-present OR user-token-absent; both refute, neither overlaps detect's path-construction failure mode.

feature: ssrf check (HTTP request to a user-controlled URL)
user_story: As a platform operator, I want outbound HTTP calls whose URL is a variable/expression to be flagged, while requests to constant literal URLs or allowlist-validated URLs pass, so that server-side request forgery introduced by an agent is caught before deploy.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='ssrf', severity='HIGH', framework='cwe-918' only when both signals agree. Signal 1 (_SSRF): a call to requests.get/post/put/head/request, urlopen, httpx.get/post, or urllib.request.urlopen up to the opening '('. Signal 2 (_verify_ssrf): inspects the argument immediately after '('  -  if it begins with a quote it is a constant URL literal and is refuted; if the line contains an allowlist guard (allowlist|allowed_hosts|whitelist|is_allowed|validate_url) it is refuted; otherwise a variable/expression is assumed and it confirms. True-positive: `r = requests.get(user_url)` fires  -  first arg is the variable user_url (test_ssrf_tp_variable_url_fires). Verify-drop: `r = requests.get("https://api.internal/v1")` is dropped because the argument is a quoted constant (test_ssrf_fp_constant_url_dropped).
edge_cases: URL built by concatenation starting with a quoted literal (`requests.get('https://' + host)`) is mis-refuted because the first char after '(' is a quote. || A validated variable URL passes only if an allowlist keyword appears on the same line; validation on a prior line is not seen. || Requests via a wrapper/session method not matching the _SSRF idioms are not detected.
notes: detect ends just after '(' specifically so verify can read the URL argument; the constant-literal and allowlist tests are the independent second signal.

feature: insecure-deserialization check (Unsafe deserialization of untrusted data)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want unsafe deserialization calls (pickle/cpickle/marshal/yaml.load/jsonpickle) on untrusted bytes to be flagged, while safe loader variants pass, so that remote-code-execution via deserialization is caught in reviewed diffs.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='insecure-deserialization', severity='HIGH', framework='cwe-502' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (_INSECURE_DESER, with the module name de-fragmented as 'pic'+'kle' so this file carries no contiguous dangerous literal): matches pickle.loads, cpickle.loads, marshal.loads, `yaml.load(`, or jsonpickle.decode. Signal 2 (_verify_insecure_deser): refutes the candidate if a safe variant appears on the line (safe_load|SafeLoader|FullLoader|literal_eval); otherwise confirms. True-positive: `obj = pickle.loads(blob)` fires  -  no safe loader present (test_insecure_deser_tp_fires). Verify-drop: `cfg = yaml.load(f, Loader=SafeLoader)` is dropped because SafeLoader is present (test_insecure_deser_fp_safe_loader_dropped).
edge_cases: yaml.load with an explicit unsafe Loader still fires (only the safe-variant tokens refute). || pickle.loads of a trusted, locally-produced blob is still flagged  -  trust of the source is not modeled. || Safe deserialization wrapped behind a custom helper name is not recognized as safe and would be flagged if it routes through a matched primitive.
notes: The safe-loader test is the independent second signal; the unsafe-deser module name is assembled from fragments to keep checks.py source clean of a contiguous dangerous literal.

feature: private-key-hardcoded check (Hard-coded private key)
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want any embedded PEM private-key header in source to be flagged as CRITICAL, while example/placeholder key blocks pass, so that leaked signing/identity keys are caught and rotated rather than slipping into the audit trail.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='private-key-hardcoded', severity='CRITICAL', framework='cwe-798' only when both signals fire. Signal 1 (_PRIVATE_KEY, assembled from fragments): matches the PEM header `-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----`. Signal 2 (_verify_private_key): refutes if the line contains an example/placeholder marker (example|dummy|placeholder|sample|test_key|fixture); otherwise confirms a real key. True-positive: `KEY = "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----..."` fires (test_private_key_tp_fires). Verify-drop: `# -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- (example placeholder)` is dropped because 'example'/'placeholder' mark it illustrative (test_private_key_fp_placeholder_dropped).
edge_cases: A genuine key on a line that also contains the word 'sample' (e.g. in a nearby comment) is suppressed by the placeholder marker. || Only the header line is detected; a key body without the matched header line is not flagged. || EC/DSA/OPENSSH variants are covered by the `[A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY` wildcard, but a non-standard header wording would be missed.
notes: The example/placeholder test is the independent second signal; the PEM header literal is de-fragmented in source. fix_hint mandates removal AND immediate rotation.

feature: cleartext-transmission check (Cleartext http:// endpoint)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want non-localhost, non-private-network http:// endpoints in source to be flagged, while https endpoints, localhost, comments, and XML/schema namespace URLs pass, so that cleartext transmission risk is caught without noise from legitimately-http identifier URLs.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='cleartext-transmission', severity='MEDIUM', framework='cwe-319' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (_CLEARTEXT, checks.py:182-184): `http://` not immediately followed by localhost|127.0.0.1|0.0.0.0|::1, an RFC1918 private host (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x), or 169.254.x link-local - a private-network/intranet http endpoint never becomes a candidate. _NS_URL matches schemas?[./] forms (checks.py:161). Signal 2 (_verify_cleartext): refutes if the line is a comment (starts with #, //, *, <!--) or matches _NS_URL (w3.org|xmlns|schemas|purl.org|/ns/|/dtd/|!doctype|example.com|example.org)  -  XML namespace/schema URLs that are legitimately http; otherwise confirms. True-positive: `API = "http://api.internal.example/v1"` fires (test_cleartext_tp_http_endpoint_fires). Verify-drop: `NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"` is dropped via _NS_URL (test_cleartext_fp_xml_namespace_dropped). True-negative: `API = "https://api.example.com"` never matches detect (test_cleartext_tn_https).
edge_cases: A real cleartext endpoint hosted on example.com is suppressed because _NS_URL treats example.(com|org) as a namespace/illustrative host. || An http:// URL inside a comment line is always refuted regardless of sensitivity. || localhost/loopback, IPv6 ::1, RFC1918 private (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x), and 169.254.x link-local http endpoints are excluded at detect-time and never become candidates (test_cleartext_fp_rfc1918_private_host_dropped).
notes: The comment + namespace test is the independent second signal that drops legitimately-http XML/schema URLs, the dominant false-positive class for this check.

feature: private-key-hardcoded? no  -  floating-action-tag check (GitHub Action pinned to a floating tag)
user_story: As a platform operator, I want CI workflow steps that pin a GitHub Action to a floating tag or branch to be flagged, while actions pinned to a full commit SHA pass, so that supply-chain tampering via mutable action references is caught per OpenSSF guidance.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='floating-action-tag', category='supply-chain', severity='MEDIUM', framework='openssf-scorecard' only when both signals agree. Signal 1 (_FLOATING_TAG): `uses: owner/repo@<ref>` in a workflow line. Signal 2 (_verify_floating_tag, checks.py:189-197): reads the ref from the DETECT match token itself (uses: owner/repo@<ref>), so a trailing comment cannot hijack it; a ref that fullmatches [0-9a-f]{7,64} (abbreviated SHA-1, full 40-hex SHA-1, or 64-hex SHA-256 pin) is refuted as safely pinned; any other non-empty ref (v1, main, master, a tag) confirms. True-positive: `- uses: actions/checkout@v4` fires because 'v4' is a floating tag (test_floating_action_tag_tp_fires). Verify-drop: `- uses: actions/checkout@<40 a's>` is dropped because the ref is a 40-char SHA (test_floating_action_tag_fp_sha_pinned_dropped); a 64-hex SHA-256 pin is likewise dropped (test_floating_action_tag_fp_sha256_pin_dropped).
edge_cases: A 7+-char lowercase-hex abbreviated commit SHA is accepted as pinned (uppercase hex still flagged). || A hex ref written in uppercase does not match [0-9a-f] and is flagged. || The ref comes from the detect match token, so a trailing comment containing '@' cannot hijack verification (test_floating_action_tag_handles_trailing_comment_with_at).
notes: The hex-pin test ([0-9a-f]{7,64}) is the independent second signal distinguishing immutable pins from mutable tags/branches. fix_hint: pin to a full 40-char commit SHA.

feature: pii-in-code check (PII literal in source: email / SSN)
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want real email addresses and US SSNs embedded in source to be flagged under GDPR data-minimisation, while example addresses and illustrative comments pass, so that personal data does not get committed and create a privacy-regime exposure.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='pii-in-code', category='privacy', severity='MEDIUM', framework='gdpr-art5-art32' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (detect): an email `[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@host.tld` OR a SSN `\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}`. Signal 2 (_verify_pii, checks.py:101-118): refutes if the email is at an RFC2606/RFC6761 reserved domain (_RESERVED_EMAIL_DOMAIN: .test/.example/.invalid TLDs plus example.com/org/net) or starts with test@/noreply@/foo@/bar@/user@example, if the line is a comment (starts with #, //, *, <!--), or - for the SSN branch - if the number falls in a never-issued SSA block (area 000/666/900+, group 00, or serial 0000); otherwise confirms a real PII literal. The detect email regex uses bounded quantifiers ({1,64}/{1,255}/{2,24}) as the SEC-4 ReDoS guard, and the SSN branch is word-bounded (checks.py:316-317). True-positive: `owner = "jane.doe@acmecorp.com"` fires  -  real domain, not a comment (test_pii_tp_real_email_fires). Verify-drop: `contact = "test@example.com"` is dropped because of example.com and the test@ prefix (test_pii_fp_example_dropped_by_verify).
edge_cases: A real address on a comment line is refuted because verify treats comments as illustrative, even if the data is genuine. || An SSN-shaped product code in a never-issued SSA block (area 000/666/9xx, group 00, serial 0000) is refuted (test_pii_ssn_fp_invalid_area_dropped); a validly-shaped number is still flagged (test_pii_ssn_tp_real_shape_fires); reserved-domain addresses are dropped (test_pii_fp_rfc2606_reserved_domain_dropped) || Addresses at non-example domains that are nonetheless synthetic (e.g. a custom test domain) are flagged.
notes: The example-address + comment test is the independent second signal that drops fixture/illustrative PII, the dominant false-positive class here.

feature: pii-credit-card check (Luhn-valid credit-card number in source)
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want 13-16 digit numbers that pass the Luhn checksum to be flagged as credit-card data (HIGH), while arbitrary numeric IDs that fail Luhn pass, so that PCI-relevant card numbers are never committed to source.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='pii-credit-card', category='privacy', severity='HIGH', framework='gdpr-art5-art32' only when both signals fire. Signal 1 (_CREDIT_CARD): a 13-16 contiguous-digit run or a grouped `dddd-dddd-dddd-dddd` form with no surrounding digits. Signal 2 (_verify_credit_card): strips all non-ASCII-digit characters ([^0-9] specifically, NOT the broad non-digit class - Unicode decimal digits are removed so they cannot corrupt the ord(ch)-48 arithmetic in _luhn_ok) and confirms only if 13<=len<=16 AND _luhn_ok(digits) passes  -  the Luhn mod-10 checksum is the independent second signal that a random ID will not satisfy. True-positive: `card = "4242424242424242"` fires because it is Luhn-valid (test_credit_card_tp_luhn_valid_fires). Verify-drop: `order_id = "1234567890123456"` is dropped because it fails the Luhn check (test_credit_card_fp_luhn_invalid_dropped).
edge_cases: A 16-digit non-card identifier that coincidentally passes Luhn would be a false positive (Luhn is necessary, not sufficient to prove it is a real card). || A card number broken across separators not matching the grouped pattern (e.g. spaces in unexpected positions) may evade detect. || Numbers adjacent to other digits are excluded by the (?<!\d)/(?!\d) boundaries, so a longer numeric blob is not partially matched. || A card written in fullwidth/Unicode digits matches detect (the detect digit class matches Unicode decimals) but is refuted after ASCII-only stripping leaves len<13 (test_credit_card_unicode_digit_does_not_corrupt_luhn).
notes: Luhn (_luhn_ok) is the independent second signal  -  a structurally card-shaped but invalid number is dropped, exactly the false-positive class the tests assert.

feature: pii-phone check (US phone number literal in source)
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want real US phone numbers in source to be flagged under data-minimisation (LOW), while reserved 555-exchange numbers, comments, and example/test/placeholder lines pass, so that genuine personal contact data is removed without flagging the documentation-safe fictional numbers.
expected_behavior: Emits check_id='pii-phone', category='privacy', severity='LOW', framework='gdpr-art5-art32' only on the two-signal gate. Signal 1 (_US_PHONE): a US-format number `(?ddd)?[-.\s]ddd[-.\s]dddd` with digit boundaries. Signal 2 (_verify_phone): refutes if the line is a comment (#, //, *, <!--), or contains example|placeholder|fake|test; otherwise strips to digits and confirms only if exactly 10 digits AND the exchange (digits[3:6]) is not '555' (the reserved/fictional exchange). True-positive: `contact = "415-867-5309"` fires  -  10 digits, exchange 867 (test_phone_tp_fires). Verify-drop: `support = "212-555-0199"` is dropped because the 555 exchange is reserved/fictional (test_phone_fp_reserved_exchange_dropped).
edge_cases: A genuine number that happens to sit on a line containing the word 'test' is suppressed by the keyword refutation. || Non-US / international formats not matching _US_PHONE are not detected. || A real number in the legacy 555 exchange range (e.g. 555-01xx is reserved, but other 555 uses existed historically) is always dropped, accepting a small false-negative to kill the dominant documentation false-positive.
notes: The 555-exchange + example/comment test is the independent second signal that drops fictional/documentation numbers, the dominant false-positive class for phone literals.

feature: MAC hash-chain append (HMAC-SHA256 keyed / SHA-256 keyless) + signed anchor
source: governance/chain.py:GovernanceChain.append (lines 80-92; _mac lines 65-69; key sourcing lines 47-53; _canonical, GENESIS); persists via store.append_chain_and_anchor (store.py:169-185)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want every governance event appended to a SHA-256 hash chain that folds in the prior entry's hash so that the audit ledger is append-only and any later tampering becomes mathematically provable rather than assumed.
expected_behavior: GovernanceChain.append(org, payload) rejects a non-dict payload with TypeError, normalizes/validates org via _tenant_key, and reads the current chain head via store.chain_head(org) -> (seq, prev_entry_hash), substituting GENESIS ('0'*64) when the org has no prior entries. It increments seq by 1, serializes the payload deterministically with _canonical (json.dumps with sort_keys=True and separators=(',',':')) into body, and computes entry_hash = _mac(key, prev_hash, body) - HMAC-SHA256 when DLE_CHAIN_KEY or DLE_CHAIN_KEY_FILE supplies the out-of-DB signing key (env value wins when both are set; SEC-6), plain SHA-256 in the keyless fallback. The chain row AND the per-org signed head/length anchor are persisted ATOMICALLY in one transaction via store.append_chain_and_anchor(org, seq, prev_hash, body, entry_hash, anchor_mac), so a crash cannot desync anchor and head. Returns {'seq': seq, 'entry_hash': entry_hash}. Because entry_hash folds in prev_hash, the chain is cryptographically linked head-to-tail and scoped per-org via the chain table's PRIMARY KEY (org, seq).
edge_cases: First append for a new org: chain_head returns (0, None), so prev_hash falls back to GENESIS ('0'*64) and the genesis entry is written at seq=1. || Two payloads with identically-valued but differently-ordered keys produce the SAME body and hash because _canonical sorts keys, so logically-equal payloads chain identically (and a re-serialization during verify reproduces the same hash). || Concurrent appends for the same org race on chain_head/seq+1; the chain table PRIMARY KEY (org, seq) makes the loser's INSERT fail rather than silently forking the chain.

feature: Chain verify / tamper-detect
user_story: As an auditor/regulator, I want to re-walk the entire hash chain and have any edited, inserted, removed, or reordered entry pinpointed so that I can independently confirm the audit trail has not been altered since it was recorded.
expected_behavior: GovernanceChain.verify(org) (chain.py:94-128) loads all rows via store.chain_rows(org) (ordered by seq ASC) and walks them with expected_seq starting at 1, carrying prev_hash initialized to GENESIS. Per-row checks: (1) row seq must equal expected_seq, else reason 'sequence gap'; (2) row prev_hash must equal the running prev_hash, else reason 'prev_hash mismatch (entry inserted/removed)'; (3) _mac(key, row prev_hash, payload) must equal entry_hash, else reason 'payload tampered (mac mismatch)'. After a clean walk it verifies the SIGNED ANCHOR: no anchor -> reason 'missing signed anchor'; an anchor whose MAC does not re-verify -> 'anchor signature invalid'; an anchor seq/head that does not match the walked head -> 'chain truncated or rolled back (anchor/head mismatch)'. EVERY return carries a 'signed' boolean (true when a chain key is configured); a fully intact chain returns {'ok': True, 'entries': len(rows), 'signed': bool}; failures return {'ok': False, 'broken_at': seq, 'reason': ..., 'signed': bool}. Hashes are recomputed from stored payloads - no stored validity flag is ever trusted.
edge_cases: Empty chain for an org: verify returns {'ok': True, 'entries': 0, 'signed': False} in keyless mode (vacuously valid). || A single edited payload leaves its entry_hash stale, so check (3) fires at that seq with reason 'payload tampered (mac mismatch)'; the first failing seq short-circuits the walk. || A deleted middle entry trips 'sequence gap'; a forged re-insertion that preserves numbering trips the prev_hash check. || Deleting the TAIL entries leaves the signed anchor pointing past the head -> 'chain truncated or rolled back (anchor/head mismatch)' is reported even though every remaining row hashes clean; keyless mode cannot catch a key-less writer forging the full tail (documented limit, SEC-6).

feature: Immutable per-change attribution
source: governance/store.py:GovernanceStore.add_change / changes (changes table: org, repo, sha, author, agent, ts, summary, n_findings)
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want each reviewed code change recorded with its author, the AI agent involved, the commit sha, and a server-stamped timestamp so that I can attribute exactly who or what produced every change and when it was governed, regardless of which AI tool generated it.
expected_behavior: GovernanceStore.add_change(org, repo, sha, author, agent, summary) inserts one row into the `changes` table (columns id AUTOINCREMENT PK, org, repo, sha, author, agent, ts, summary, n_findings DEFAULT 0), stamps ts = time.time() server-side (the caller cannot supply it), commits, and returns the integer lastrowid as the change_id. Attribution fields (author = human, agent = AI agent name) are stored side-by-side so a change is attributable to a human, an agent, or both, making the layer agent-agnostic. set_change_findings(org, change_id, n) (store.py:111-114) later updates only the n_findings counter, org-scoped (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND org=?) so a change id belonging to another tenant is a no-op; add_change normalizes/validates org via _tenant_key. changes(org, repo=None) reads back rows for the org (optionally filtered by repo) ordered by ts DESC, id DESC and returns them as a list of dicts; an org/repo index (idx_changes_org) backs the lookup. There is no update path for author/agent/sha/ts and no delete method, so the attribution record is effectively immutable once written.
edge_cases: A pure-human commit with no AI involved stores agent as NULL (and vice-versa for an agent-only change with author NULL); both columns are nullable, so attribution degrades gracefully instead of being rejected. || sha may be NULL (uncommitted/working-tree diff) yet the change is still recorded and attributable by author/agent/ts. || Two changes with the same wall-clock ts are disambiguated in the changes() listing by the secondary 'id DESC' sort, so newest-by-insertion still wins ordering.

feature: Changes + findings storage incl. severity_counts
source: governance/store.py:GovernanceStore.add_finding / findings / severity_counts (findings table; idx_findings_org on org,repo,severity)
user_story: As a platform operator, I want every safety finding stored with its check, category, severity, location, grounding citation, and verified flag, and rolled up into per-severity counts so that I can surface an org's risk posture at a glance and drill into the individual evidence behind each number.
expected_behavior: GovernanceStore.add_finding(change_id, org, repo, finding) inserts one row into the `findings` table, requiring finding['check_id'], finding['category'], and finding['severity'] (KeyError if absent) and optionally pulling file, line, snippet, framework, framework_url, clause via finding.get(...). The verified flag is normalized to 1/0 from finding.get('verified', True) (default True -> 1), ts is server-stamped via time.time(), the insert is committed, and the new finding id is returned. findings(org, repo=None) returns the stored rows as dicts ordered by ts DESC, id DESC (optionally repo-filtered). severity_counts(org) runs SELECT severity, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY severity and returns a dict mapping each severity string to its count (e.g. {'CRITICAL': 2, 'HIGH': 5}); the composite index idx_findings_org on (org, repo, severity) backs both the filtered listing and the grouped roll-up. The framework/framework_url/clause columns carry the grounding citation so each counted finding is traceable to its compliance source.
edge_cases: An org with no findings: severity_counts returns {} (empty dict, not zero-filled per level), so callers must treat a missing severity key as zero. || A finding dict missing 'check_id'/'category'/'severity' raises KeyError at insert time (fail-fast), enforcing that every stored finding is fully classified; optional metadata fields silently default to NULL. || Severity strings are stored verbatim with no enum constraint, so case/spelling drift (e.g. 'High' vs 'HIGH') would produce separate buckets in severity_counts; the n_findings counter on the parent change is maintained separately via set_change_findings and is not auto-incremented by add_finding.
notes: severity_counts tally/empty-org/org-scoping and the add_finding KeyError-on-missing-severity are proven directly at the store level (test_severity_counts_tallies_by_severity, test_severity_counts_empty_org_is_empty_dict, test_severity_counts_is_org_scoped, test_add_finding_requires_severity).

feature: Org governance report (markdown)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want a single markdown report rolling up what my people are building and what's risky, so that I can review agent and human activity and chain integrity in one human-readable artifact without parsing raw JSON.
expected_behavior: org_report(store, chain, org) calls org_summary() then returns a single newline-joined ASCII markdown string. Structure (in order): an H1 title '# Agent-governance report - org: {org}'; a blockquote coverage-honesty line ('Absence of a finding is not proof of safety...'); a '## What your people are making' section reporting '{changes} change(s) across {len(repos)} repo(s): {comma-joined repos or (none)}', followed by per-agent indented bullets sorted by descending change count (key=lambda kv: -kv[1]); a '## Safety findings' section that prints '- none surfaced by the current checks' when findings is empty, otherwise emits per-severity count lines walking _SEVERITY_ORDER=(CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM,LOW) skipping zero counts, then a '### Detail' subsection listing up to the first 50 findings as '- [{severity}] {check_id} | {file}:{line} | {framework} | `{snippet}`'; and a '## Audit-trail integrity' section that forks on chk['signed'] (report.py:68-83): signed -> '- [OK] tamper-evident chain intact, HMAC-signed ({entries} entries)' plus an explicit rollback-limit line (an external witness is needed to catch a rollback by a key-holding writer); keyless -> '- [OK] chain intact, SHA-256 linked ({entries} entries) - set DLE_CHAIN_KEY for tamper-evidence'; broken -> '- [BROKEN] chain broken at entry {broken_at}: {reason} - the record may have been altered'. When more than 50 findings exist, the Detail header announces the truncation via '(showing first 50 of N)' (report.py:61-62). Output is deliberately ASCII-only (no emoji/typographic punctuation) so it renders identically on any console including Windows cp1252.
edge_cases: Empty org: zero changes, zero repos (renders '(none)'), zero findings (renders 'none surfaced by the current checks') - report still produces all four sections plus an intact-chain line for an empty chain. || More than 50 findings: only the first 50 are rendered in '### Detail' (s['findings'][:50]) while the per-severity counts above reflect all findings via severity_counts - truncation is announced via '(showing first 50 of N)', not silent. || A change with a null/empty agent is bucketed under 'unknown' in by_agent before sorting.
notes: Severity count lines come from store.severity_counts(org) (key 'sev'), while the detail list and total come from store.findings(org); the two can diverge if a severity is present in counts but its findings fall outside the first-50 slice.

feature: Org summary (machine-readable JSON rollup)
user_story: As a platform operator, I want a JSON-able summary object of an org's changes, agents, severities, findings, and chain status, so that I can feed governance state into dashboards, alerting, or downstream tooling programmatically.
expected_behavior: org_summary(store, chain, org) returns a dict with exactly these keys: 'org' (the org string echoed back), 'changes' (int count = len(store.changes(org))), 'repos' (a sorted, de-duplicated list built from a set comprehension {c['repo'] for c in changes}), 'by_agent' (dict mapping agent->int change count, with a null/empty agent coalesced to 'unknown'), 'severity_counts' (passthrough of store.severity_counts(org)), 'findings' (passthrough list of store.findings(org), full, not truncated), and 'chain' (passthrough of chain.verify(org)). It performs no I/O of its own beyond the store/chain calls and is the single source feeding org_report(); the agent-count loop initializes missing keys via by_agent.get(a, 0) + 1.
edge_cases: Empty org: 'changes'=0, 'repos'=[], 'by_agent'={}, 'findings'=[], and 'chain' reflects an empty-but-valid chain. || Multiple changes whose 'agent' field is None all collapse into a single 'unknown' bucket rather than separate entries. || 'repos' is sorted and unique even when many changes share repos or arrive out of order, so the list is deterministic regardless of insertion order.
notes: 'findings' here is the FULL list (unlike report.py detail's [:50] slice and dashboard's [:100] slice); consumers needing every finding should read org_summary, not the rendered markdown. The exact key set, sorted+deduped repos, and agent=None -> by_agent['unknown'] coalescing are asserted directly by the contract test.

feature: Self-contained HTML governance dashboard render
user_story: As an org security lead, I want a self-contained HTML dashboard of agent activity and risk that opens in any browser, so that I can share a visual governance snapshot with stakeholders without standing up a server or external assets.
expected_behavior: render_dashboard(store, chain, org) calls dashboard_data() and returns one complete HTML document string rendered as a VERIFICATION INSTRUMENT (the dashboard redesign, dashboard.py module docstring): a verdict chip (SIGNED / KEYLESS / BROKEN tri-state); the standing coverage-honesty disclaimer ('absence of a finding is not proof of safety') rendered BEFORE any numbers; a coverage panel as the hero - every check in the CHECKS registry shown fired-vs-quiet ('N of TOTAL', registry imported from checks.py), with out-of-registry findings excluded from the denominator and surfaced as off-registry chips; an on-screen audit ledger of the actual chain rows from store.chain_rows(org) (seq plus truncated-mono prev_hash/entry_hash, linkage re-walk mirroring chain.verify's broken_at, rows after a break rendered 'void after break'); a per-entry canonical-payload recompute block demonstrating the payload carries no snippet (redaction holds); a traceability drill path (change -> findings -> chain seq, see RPT-6); per-finding two-signal reasoning + framework/clause/URL citation + redacted evidence + fix hint; a keyed 'LIVE' vs 'dormant: no DLE_CHAIN_KEY' contrast; and a Limits section. dashboard_data keeps all prior keys and ADDS chain_rows and coverage (plus per-change groups); the findings render is capped at 100 with a visible 'Showing the first 100 of N' cap note. All dynamic values are escaped via _esc, and hrefs are gated to http(s) by _safe_href (javascript: URLs neutralized).
edge_cases: Empty org: the coverage panel shows every registry check quiet, the ledger is empty, the verdict reflects the keyless/signed mode, and the disclaimer still renders before any numbers. || A finding whose check_id is not in the CHECKS registry is excluded from the coverage denominator and shown as an off-registry chip rather than silently inflating coverage. || Rows recorded after a chain break render 'void after break' instead of a green link; malicious content in org/snippet/reason is neutralized by _esc and javascript: hrefs by _safe_href.
notes: dashboard_data exposes chain_rows/coverage for JSON consumers. The render is self-contained except an optional Google-Fonts (IBM Plex) stylesheet link that degrades to system fonts - 'no external assets' no longer strictly holds. feature: Compliance posture report with control-coverage count
user_story: As a compliance officer, I want a report mapping our governance posture to cited control families with a count of distinct control areas covered, so that I can present framework-grounded evidence (CIS v8, NIST CSF/SSDF, plus finding-cited frameworks) during an audit.
expected_behavior: compliance_report(store, chain, org) calls compliance_data() and returns a newline-joined ASCII markdown string. compliance_data builds 'control_areas' by counting findings per f['framework'] (missing coalesced to '(ungrounded)') with each framework's URL, ordered by Counter.most_common(); 'mechanism_controls' from the 20 static MECHANISM_CONTROLS entries (compliance.py:50-71) spanning 10 cited frameworks resolved through COMPLIANCE_FRAMEWORKS (compliance.py:35-46: CIS v8, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SSDF, SOC 2 TSC, FDA Part 11, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 42001, GDPR, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF); and 'control_coverage' = len of the set union of _canonical_framework-normalized tokens from finding-cited framework labels and mechanism framework ids (compliance.py:92-129), so a framework cited both as a finding label and a mechanism id (e.g. GDPR) counts ONCE. The report renders: H1 title; a blockquote disclaimer ('governance evidence, not a compliance certification'); a Scope line with the distinct-control-coverage count; the control-areas section (or '- no findings (no control gaps surfaced by the current checks)'); the mechanism-controls section; an Audit-trail integrity section that forks signed/keyless (HMAC-signed wording vs 'set DLE_CHAIN_KEY') or BROKEN (compliance.py:170-176); and the Pending section. Only mappings backed by a verified citation are asserted.
edge_cases: Zero findings: control_areas is empty so the section prints the 'no control gaps surfaced' line, yet control_coverage is still non-zero because the 10 mechanism frameworks seed the covered set. || Findings missing a 'framework' key are bucketed under '(ungrounded)' and counted as a distinct area with a non-authoritative label. || A finding framework label that overlaps a mechanism framework is deduped through _canonical_framework so it counts once (test_control_coverage_does_not_double_count_gdpr_id_vs_name) - coverage counts distinct canonical frameworks, not finding volume.
notes: control_coverage is a distinct-canonical-framework count via the _CROSS_NAMESPACE_REGIME/_canonical_framework normalization (compliance.py:92-129), NOT a sum of findings; a broken chain flips the integrity section to 'evidence integrity COMPROMISED' but does not change the coverage count. ISO provenance is honestly worded: two ISO ids are cross-checked, not primary (iso.org blocks automated fetch; compliance.py:26-34).

feature: Pending-regimes honesty line

This enforces the anti-citation-theater discipline: what this layer cannot evidence is surfaced honestly rather than silently omitted or over-claimed.

feature: CLI ingest (record + scan a change into the audit trail)
user_story: As an org security lead, I want to record every code change with its author and originating agent and have it scanned and committed to the tamper-evident trail, so that I have a single durable system-of-record for who/what changed code and what safety findings it triggered.
expected_behavior: `dle-govern ingest --org ORG --repo REPO --diff-file PATH [--author A] [--agent G] [--sha S]` opens the store + GovernanceChain via _open(args.db), reads the unified diff (file path, or '-' for stdin via _read_diff), builds an Attribution(author=args.author or 'unknown', agent=args.agent or 'human'), and calls ingest_change(store, chain, org, repo, diff, attr, sha=sha). It prints the result dict as indented JSON with the 'findings' key stripped out (so change_id, n_findings, chain_seq, files, etc. are shown), then prints each finding on its own line as `  [SEVERITY] check_id  file:line  | framework`. Exits 0 on any successful ingest regardless of findings (non-gating); a missing/unreadable --diff-file exits nonzero via a clean one-line SystemExit message from _read_diff (cli.py:32-41; no traceback, and diff files are read with errors='replace' so non-UTF-8 bytes never crash the read), and a blank/invisible/|-containing --org fails with ValueError from _tenant_key inside ingest_change before any DB write. DB path defaults to DLE_GOV_DB env or '.governance/governance.db'.
edge_cases: --author / --agent omitted: attribution defaults to author='unknown', agent='human' rather than erroring, so a human commit and an unlabeled agent commit are still recorded. || --diff-file '-' reads the entire diff from stdin (CI piping a git diff) instead of a file path. || A clean diff with zero findings still records a change and advances the chain; the findings loop simply prints nothing and exit stays 0. || Missing/unreadable --diff-file: clean nonzero exit with no traceback (test_cli_missing_diff_file_clean_nonzero_exit).
notes: ingest is the write path and is deliberately non-gating (exit 0); the gating sibling is `scan` (IFC-2). stdout/stderr are reconfigured to UTF-8 in main() so scanned non-ASCII content never crashes a cp1252 console.

feature: CLI scan as a CI gate (non-zero exit on HIGH/CRITICAL, no DB write)
user_story: As a developer, I want a dry safety scan of my diff that fails the build only when a HIGH or CRITICAL issue is present, so that I get a fast pre-merge gate without polluting the org's audit trail on every local run.
expected_behavior: `dle-govern scan --diff-file PATH` reads the diff (file or '-' stdin), iterates parse_diff(diff) to get (path, added_lines) tuples, and extends a findings list with scan_lines(path, added) per file. It does NOT open the store or chain and writes nothing to the DB. For each finding it prints `[SEVERITY] check_id  file:line  | framework` and a second line `    fix: <fix_hint>`, then prints `\n{N} finding(s)`. Exit code is 1 if any finding has severity in ('CRITICAL','HIGH'), else 0  -  making it usable directly as a CI gate / git pre-push hook.
edge_cases: Only MEDIUM/LOW (or informational) findings present: they are printed but exit code stays 0, so the build is not blocked. || Empty or non-diff input: parse_diff yields no added lines, '0 finding(s)' is printed, exit 0. || scan never touches the store, so it is safe to run on a developer laptop with no .governance DB and produces no chain mutation. || A missing/unreadable --diff-file exits nonzero with a clean one-line error via the shared _read_diff helper (test_cli_missing_diff_file_clean_nonzero_exit), not a traceback.
notes: This is the only command whose exit code encodes a pass/fail gate decision; contrast with verify-chain (IFC-4) which gates on chain integrity. The HIGH/CRITICAL threshold is hardcoded in the exit expression on line 52.

feature: CLI verify-chain (tamper-evident audit chain integrity gate)
user_story: As an auditor/regulator, I want to independently verify that an organization's governance audit chain has not been altered, with a non-zero exit when the chain is broken, so that I can trust the record as evidence and wire integrity checks into automated monitoring.
expected_behavior: `dle-govern verify-chain --org ORG` opens store + chain and calls chain.verify(org), which returns a result dict containing at least an 'ok' boolean. It prints the full result as indented JSON and returns exit code 0 if res['ok'] is True, else 1. A broken/altered chain therefore both surfaces detail in the JSON and fails the command, so CI or a cron monitor can alarm on it. The result JSON includes signed:true/false; in keyless mode the command prints a stderr warning that keyless verification only catches accidental edits and DLE_CHAIN_KEY should be set (cli.py:74-81). Broken-chain reasons include the anchor family: missing signed anchor / anchor signature invalid / chain truncated or rolled back (chain.py:121-127).
edge_cases: Empty chain (org with no changes yet): verify is expected to return ok=True (a trivially intact empty chain) and exit 0. || Any post-hoc edit to a recorded row breaks the hash linkage -> ok=False -> exit 1, which is the intended tamper alarm. || The JSON body carries the diagnostic detail (e.g. which sequence broke), so the non-zero exit is actionable rather than opaque. || Truncation/rollback of the chain tail is caught via the signed anchor (reason: 'chain truncated or rolled back'), not just per-row hashing.
notes: This is the integrity counterpart to scan's safety gate (IFC-2). DEPLOY.md frames it as the canonical way to prove the SQLite audit trail is untampered; the dashboard also surfaces a chain banner from the same chain.verify.
